\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Foundation models for time series~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, ansari2024chronos, liu2025timerxl, liu2024timer, woo2024moirai, lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm, cohen2025toto, liu2025sundial, jin2024timellm, zhou2023onefitsall, liu2024autotimes, pan2024s2ipllm, liu2024unitime, shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1} are deployed by freezing the encoder and training a tiny per-task adapter on top, so one backbone can serve many tenants through hot-swapped heads (App.~\ref{app:deployment}). The adapter is therefore the object a practitioner actually ships; this paper studies its design, holding the backbone fixed.

Today's adapters apply a single fixed pooling rule (mean-pool, last-token, etc.) to every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a). The shape information that distinguishes one window from the next, however, lives in different hidden-state subspaces from window to window~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}, and no one rule reads them all well. The obvious remedy is a per-window dispatcher that picks among topologically distinct readers~\citep{wang2022adamix}, an AdaMix-style mixture-of-experts (MoE) head.

This head looks unremarkable, yet on every TSFM whose encoder begins with an instance normalizer it degenerates as soon as a single transformer block is unfrozen for joint training (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}b): the gating mass over experts contracts to one-hot within tens of optimizer steps (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}), the favored expert's gradients reshape the backbone to serve it alone (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}), and the silenced experts never receive a learning signal. We name the phenomenon \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} and trace it upstream of the optimizer: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} subtracts each window's mean and variance before the encoder, so the per-window statistics that would have made experts distinguishable are structurally absent from the hidden states the router reads (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}). Eleven standard MoE rescues, namely load balancing, Z-loss, ReMoE, expert choice, top-$k$ sharpening, and seven more ($720$ runs in total), close only $10.9\%$ of the MSE gap that the input-side intervention closes ($2.7\times$ shortfall, Table~\ref{tab:rescue}); Moirai, whose I/O scaling is not learnable-affine, does not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}), narrowing the cause to learnable-affine encoder normalization.

The fix prescribed by the diagnosis modifies a single wire: route on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$, the input \emph{before} the encoder strips its statistics, while leaving experts, optimizer, and a now strictly frozen backbone untouched. We call the resulting head \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA). The same diagnosis predicts that joint training should hurt rather than help here, since backbone updates only ever serve a single live expert, a \emph{Frozen Paradox} (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}) we confirm empirically (frozen wins on $4/6$ datasets; unfreezing never recovers more than $13\%$).

The collapse $\to$ mechanism $\to$ minimal-fix arc structures our three contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
\item \textbf{Problem.} We frame routing collapse on instance-normalized TSFMs as a router-\emph{input} pathology, distinct from and upstream of the optimization-side collapse pathologies that prior MoE work targets~\citep{fedus2022switch, zoph2022stmoe, wang2025remoe, zhou2022expertchoice}. The dichotomy predicts which interventions can and cannot work: the optimization-side rescues above leave $89\%$ of the gap on the table that the input-side fix closes.
\item \textbf{Mechanism.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) makes precise which information about the input is removed before the router sees it. From it we derive $R(\mathcal{D})$, a training-free signal-ratio practitioners can compute from raw dataset statistics; it anti-correlates with collapse risk at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$) across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality, and correctly abstains on the boundary case (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$).
\item \textbf{Method.} RR-MoA changes only the router's input. It dominates the AdaMix baseline on every cell of the primary benchmark ($54/54$ wins, $26$--$79\%$ MSE), beats LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning at $p{<}0.001$, and is not subsumed by naively re-injecting $(\mu,\sigma)$ ($+42$--$239\%$ MSE; $11/18$ cells re-collapse). Two architecturally distinct instantiations confirm the principle is broader than the specific router: \textbf{SR-MoA} replaces the external router with per-expert sigmoids ($+13$--$42\%$ over RR-MoA on six datasets), and \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} carries the raw-input principle into each expert's body, closing the DLinear gap across six backbones $\times$ four horizons.
\end{itemize}
